title: Gotrade Daily: US Inflation Cools, Big Banks Post Records
summary: US inflation cooled to 3.5% and Wall Street rose. Five big banks opened Q2 earnings, Goldman posting a record. ASML and Morgan Stanley report tonight.
body_text: At the same time, Q2 earnings season opened with five big US banks reporting at once. All beat estimates, though their stock reactions split. Tonight's Watchlist 📈 Stock Movement (14 Jul earnings reaction) What to Watch Goldman Sachs ( GS ) +7.6% Best quarter on record, equities trading revenue set a record. Watch the durability of investment-banking momentum. JPMorgan ( JPM ) +2% Record profit, helped by a $4.6B gain on its Visa stake. Watch second-half NII guidance. Bank of America ( BAC ) +1.9% EPS $1.21 beat the $1.12 estimate, profit up 27%. The most rate-sensitive name. Wells Fargo ( WFC ) +0.6% EPS $2.00 topped the $1.72 estimate, extending its post-asset-cap recovery. Citigroup ( C ) -4.2% Best revenue in a decade, but the stock fell on cautious second-half spending guidance. Tonight's Catalysts 🧨 ASML is the bellwether for AI chip spending ASML reports before the open. Demand for its EUV lithography tools is a signal for the entire AI semiconductor supply chain. Strong order numbers could ease fears that the AI rally has outrun its fundamentals, the same worry that pressured Arm and Korean chip stocks a day earlier. Morgan Stanley and BlackRock are next Morgan Stanley (wealth-management flows and investment-banking fees) and BlackRock (AUM and ETF inflows) carry the bank-earnings story forward tonight. Strong results could extend the positive sentiment set by Goldman and JPMorgan.

title: The Role of Patient Engagement in Medical Billing and RCM
summary: Crucial in RCM and operations, patient financial engagement means providing info, tools, and support patients need to understand and pay medical bills.
body_text: Picture the ideal patient visit: intake is simple, the appointment starts on time, provider is attentive, and the quality of care is excellent. By every measure of clinical effectiveness and patient experience, the visit is a success. But two weeks later, a bill arrives in the mail. Charges are higher than expected. Some line items don’t match the explanation of benefits (EOB). When the patient calls to ask about the charges, they’re on hold for several minutes. When they reach the billing or patient support team, they get voicemail. When they finally connect, the staff member lacks the information they need to fully explain the balance. Even if the rest of the experience is top-notch, poor patient billing experiences like this erode trust and impact key downstream metrics: satisfaction scores, payment rates, retention, and revenue. More than simply billing inconveniences, these are failures of patient engagement . And they’re far more common than they should be: 45% of insured, working-age adults received a medical bill or were charged a copay for a service they thought should have been covered by their insurance . ‍ Nearly 70% of U.S. adults with private health insurance report receiving an unexpected medical bill — and of those, more than 30% were unable to pay the bill with money immediately available to them. When providers prioritize and improve patient engagement, the results show across the board: patient satisfaction is higher, health outcomes improve, operations are more efficient, and the speed and rate of patient payments increase significantly. ‍ What Is Patient Engagement? Patient engagement is the process of actively involving patients in their own healthcare journey — not just in clinical decisions, but in every touchpoint that shapes their experience with a provider. Patient engagement occurs from the moment a patient schedules an appointment to the moment they pay their final bill. It directly impacts patient satisfaction, trust, and the overall patient experience. ‍ What Is Patient Financial Engagement? Patient financial engagement is the process of communicating with patients about the financial side of healthcare — providing the information, tools, and support needed to understand and pay medical bills. These workflows determine the difference between a patient who ignores a confusing statement and one who pays their bill promptly because the process was clear and convenient. ‍ Why Does Patient Engagement Matter? At its most basic level, patient-provider relationships depend on trust and mutual engagement. When patients are more engaged in their care, patient satisfaction is higher, and health outcomes improve . In addition to clinical benefits, patient engagement yields significant financial benefits, which are critical at a time when patient responsibility and out-of-pocket costs are at their highest . Patient engagement matters to patients, provider organizations, and staff for varying reasons: ‍ The Patient Side Patients who feel informed and supported are more likely to return to the same provider. When patients are better educated about their financial responsibility and have easy access to billing FAQs, there are fewer surprise bills and billing disputes. Thus, patient-provider communication around billing is extremely important. The quality of explanations matters (clear EOBs and statements, plain-language descriptions), and so do consistency and breadth across channels : email, phone, text, and print. Practices that truly excel also personalize the experience – customizing outreach based on demographics or balance size. For example, a practice may reach out in different languages, send more texts to certain patients, or offer payment plans to patients that owe higher balances. Higher quality patient engagement translates to improved patient satisfaction and a better overall experience . Patients should have easy, immediate access to answers to common billing questions, regardless of how or when they reach out. ‍ The Provider Side For providers, higher patient engagement streamlines healthcare operations and RCM workflows . Engaged patients pay more bills overall (increasing revenue capture) and pay sooner (boosting cash flow and point-of-service collections). A more engaged patient population means higher patient retention and increased referrals. When each patient represents significant lifetime value to a healthcare practice, even small improvements in patient engagement impact the long-term financial stability of the practice. Consider this example from Medical Economics : ‍ “If a practice prevents one no-show and can fill one open appointment a day, that could result in an additional $200-$300 a day in revenue for the average provider. If the practice has 1,500 active patients, and they can increase that by 10% through patient referrals, they increase revenue by $75,000 a year." ‍ Implementing a few key patient engagement improvements — like automated appointment reminders, self-service appointment scheduling, and online payment options — can significantly impact revenue. These gains create the margin needed to enable new growth, whether that’s expanding a geographic footprint, adding services, or investing in new technology. ‍ The Employee Side The right patient engagement technology streamlines operational workflows , improving the employee experience. When patients are better informed upfront, staff spend less time on repetitive, manual tasks: answering the same billing questions, chasing down payments, or resolving billing disputes. Better-informed patients are also less frustrated and less likely to have negative or combative interactions with staff. Fewer questions lead to less work managing inboxes and answering phones. Staff can then redirect their time to more complex cases, insurance follow-up, and higher-value work that elsewhere improves the organization’s bottom line, or improves patient outcomes. ‍ What Patients Expect from Providers The consumerization of healthcare is reshaping patient expectations. Patients today compare their healthcare experience not just to other providers, but to the seamless digital experiences they have with banks, retailers, and other apps. Patients expect convenience, transparency, and a personalized experience that treats them as an individual. But there is still a troubling gap between what patients want and what providers can deliver. When practices rely on outdated engagement technology like that provided by most EHRs , patients notice. According to the 2024 Trends in Healthcare Payments report from J.P. Morgan, 75% of consumers want to pay medical bills online, yet 71% of providers still collect from patients using paper and manual processes . Meanwhile, 50% of providers were challenged by large patient balances. ‍ When interacting with their providers, patients expect: Trust and transparency Patients want to trust their provider — and that trust extends to the financial side of care. They expect not to be surprised by unforeseen bills, and they want upfront cost estimates so they can plan for their healthcare expenses. Investment in their care Patients want to feel engaged in their healthcare journey, not just processed through a system. They want access to their medical records, lab results, and the ability to communicate with their providers through modern, easy-to-use interfaces. Financial education and support Patients want to be educated about healthcare costs, insurance coverage, and payment options. They want to understand their financial responsibilities and have support navigating the billing process. Patients want clear, concise billing statements that explain what portion of their bill is covered by insurance and what they owe. Convenience and personalization Patients want multiple payment options (online, in-person, over the phone), the ability to set up payment plans, and communication through their preferred channels. They expect proactive, timely communication about their financial obligations — not a bill that arrives weeks or months after the fact. ‍ True patient engagement goes beyond clinical effectiveness to include financial operations like medical billing, coding, and revenue cycle management (RCM). When the clinical, operational, and interpersonal elements work together, they deliver measurable results: Patients with high levels of trust in their provider are more likely to recommend them to others — a direct driver of referral-based growth. And practices that invest in patient-friendly billing and payment systems see faster payments, higher collection rates, and fewer billing disputes. ‍ How to Prioritize and Improve Patient Engagement Meeting patient expectations requires improvements in communication, technology, and billing . The most effective patient engagement strategies don’t treat these as siloed initiatives — they build an integrated system where each reinforces the others. ‍ 1. Patient Communication and Price Transparency The No Surprises Act and CMS price transparency rules require providers to make pricing information available to patients. But beyond legal compliance, transparency is a trust-builder. When patients understand what they’ll owe before a visit, they’re far less likely to delay payment or abandon a bill after the fact. Effective price transparency is part of a larger patient communication strategy that spans the entire care journey: Before the visit: Collect patient information and insurance details, provide accurate cost estimates to set expectations, verify eligibility (both when the appointment is set and again just before the visit to catch changes), and send appointment reminders to reduce no-shows and lost revenue. Day of the visit: Streamline check-in by having patients fill their own information, and equip staff to collect the right payment at the point of service . Payment rates decline sharply after patients leave the office, so being prepared to discuss and collect balances, and enable AutoPay at the time of service is crucial. After the visit: Provide claim status updates, deliver clear final billing, communicate directly about any outstanding balance, and automate payment reminders through the patient’s preferred channel. Streamlined payment workflows, ideally without requiring a login, make it easy for patients to act immediately. Communication also means meeting patients where they are. That means offering outreach via email, text, phone, and print — and allowing patients to choose their preferred method. Automated reminders can improve payment rates while also reducing no-shows, a dual benefit that directly impacts revenue. ‍ 2. Patient Engagement Tools and Technology The rise of AI in healthcare RCM is rapidly advancing the tools available to improve patient engagement. Providers can automate recurring, rules-based tasks that once required hours of manual staff effort, while simultaneously delivering a more personalized and responsive experience for patients. Key technology capabilities that support patient engagement in billing: System integrations that connect billing platforms with EHRs and practice management systems, ensuring account balances are updated in real time across systems and reducing manual reconciliation. The best integrations provide bidirectional (both read & write) functionality. Omnichannel communication tools that enable two-way communication through text, email, and chat — for example, sending a secure text with a direct link to the patient’s statement or a reminder of what’s due that month. When patients can access their account directly, without the need to enter a username or remember a password, the result is a faster, more intuitive payment experience. AI-powered billing support that provides 24/7 answers to common billing questions, processes payments, and enrolls patients in payment plans without requiring staff intervention. Payment prediction and analytics that help finance teams proactively identify patients who may have difficulty paying and offer payment plan options before a balance goes to collections. Multilingual support that ensures all patients can understand their bills and communicate with their provider’s billing team, regardless of language preference. These tools reduce errors in medical billing and insurance claims while also increasing patient satisfaction . And the need is urgent: fewer than half of those who encountered billing errors challenged them, and the most common reason was that patients simply didn’t know they had the right to do so, particularly among younger and low-income patients. Technology that proactively surfaces clear, accurate billing information can help close this gap before it becomes a collection problem. ‍ 3. Billing Enablement and Education It should be as easy as possible for patients to pay. That means implementing card-on-file programs during patient access workflows, consolidating all charges into a single, clear transaction where feasible, and offering secure, no-login-required payment workflows that eliminate friction. Providers should offer multiple and flexible payment options — taking payments easily in the office, over the phone, and online — and use automated phone payment options and convenient statements with integrated payment links. But ease of payment is only half the equation. Patients also need to understand their bills. Billing enablement and education should address: ‍ Itemized, clear statements that explain charges in plain language, both at the point of service and after the visit. Statements should match the insurance explanation of benefits (EOB) to reduce confusion. Practices should also consider removing paper-based processes where possible — encouraging patients to opt in for electronic statements and digital payment methods , which reduce costs and speed up payments. Immediate answers to billing questions . Patients shouldn’t have to wait until business hours or navigate a phone tree to understand their bill. AI-powered tools like Billie can provide instant, context-aware answers to patient billing questions around the clock. Access to financial counseling . For patients facing larger balances or complex insurance situations, offering financial counseling can make the difference between a paid bill and one that goes to collections. Education on healthcare costs and key financial terms . Deductibles, copays, coinsurance, and out-of-pocket maximums can be confusing for many patients — especially when insurance policies change or deductibles reset at the beginning of the year . Proactive education helps patients plan for these transitions. Staff training . Employees are the front line of the billing experience. Invest in training staff on RCM concepts, terminology, and workflows , as well as customer service and communication skills. Staff should be empathetic, able to answer billing questions thoroughly, and trained to partner with patients to figure out the best approach to payment. When a patient calls with a question about their bill, staff should take the time to answer and ensure the patient understands before ending the conversation. Actively seeking patient feedback — through patient satisfaction surveys or by paying attention to concerns patients raise when contacting the office — helps teams continuously improve. Setting clear expectations on billing timelines . Patients should know when and how bills will arrive. Proactive communication about what to expect — and when — prevents confusion and builds trust. Providers should also track and measure KPIs to understand what is working and what can be improved in the payment process. ‍ Patient Engagement & RCM Patient engagement starts with the right technology and the workflows to leverage it. Collectly is a leading RCM and patient engagement platform that applies advanced automation and agentic AI to the full patient financial journey. It integrates with any EHR/PM system and enables practices to efficiently reach patients on text, email, voice, and paper mail with clear statements and convenient, modern payment options. Across 3,000+ practices, the Collectly platform has achieved 95% patient satisfaction, a 2-3x increase in collections, and saved 66% on cost-to-collect.

title: Benefits of Fire-Resistant Hydraulic Fluids and Why Viscosity Matters
summary: Hydraulic fluids are essential to the smooth operation of many types of machinery—from forklifts and hydraulic cranes to scissor lifts and pallet jacks. But what exactly do hydraulic fluids do, and why does it matter if they’re fire-resistant, synthetic, o
body_text: The Benefits of Fire-Resistant Hydraulic Fluids and Why Viscosity & Synthetic Matter Hydraulic fluids are essential to the smooth operation of many types of machinery—from forklifts and hydraulic cranes to scissor lifts and pallet jacks. But what exactly do hydraulic fluids do, and why does it matter if they’re fire-resistant, synthetic, or of a specific viscosity? This article breaks down these key concepts in an approachable way and explains why choosing the right fluid, like QUINTOLUBRIC® 888-46 , can protect your equipment and improve performance. What Are Hydraulic Fluids Used For? Hydraulic fluid plays several critical roles in hydraulic systems, including: · Energy Transfer Medium: It transmits power through hydraulic machinery, enabling movement and force. · Lubricant: It reduces friction between metal components, preventing wear. · Sealant: It helps maintain system pressure by sealing clearances. · Coolant: It dissipates heat generated by equipment operation. · Contaminant Carrier: It transports dirt, metal particles, and other debris away from critical components. Together, these functions help keep machines running reliably and efficiently under demanding conditions. Understanding Hydraulic Fluid Viscosity and Why It Matters Viscosity refers to a fluid’s thickness or resistance to flow. Think of honey versus water—honey is more viscous because it flows more slowly. For hydraulic fluids, viscosity is critical because it impacts: · Energy Efficiency: Fluids that are too thick can cause excess energy loss, while fluids that are too thin may fail to lubricate properly. · Equipment Protection: Correct viscosity forms a protective film between metal surfaces, reducing wear. Temperature Performance: Viscosity changes with temperature; fluids must maintain performance in both cold start-ups and high-heat operations Low vs. High Viscosity Hydraulic Fluids · Low Viscosity Fluids are used in cold environments or applications requiring quick fluid flow, such as fast-acting controls. · High Viscosity Fluids provide better cushioning and protection under heavy loads or high-temperature conditions. Choosing the right viscosity fluid helps extend equipment life and ensures smooth operation. What Does Synthetic Hydraulic Fluid Mean and Why Is It Important? Synthetic hydraulic fluids are engineered from chemically refined base oils and specialized additives. Compared to conventional mineral-based oils, synthetics offer: · Enhanced Thermal Stability: They resist breakdown at higher temperatures. · Improved Oxidation Resistance: This leads to longer fluid life. · Better Low-Temperature Performance: Synthetics maintain viscosity in cold conditions. · Reduced Deposits: Cleaner operation with fewer sludge and varnish issues. These properties make synthetic fluids ideal for demanding environments where reliability and longevity are crucial. In many industrial settings, hydraulic systems operate near heat or open flames—think steel mills, foundries, or mining operations. Here, fire-resistant hydraulic fluids are a must. What Is Fire-Resistant Hydraulic Fluid? Fire-resistant hydraulic fluids are specially formulated to resist ignition and minimize fire risk. They achieve this through base fluids and additives that inhibit combustion even if exposed to sparks or flames. Why Fire Resistance Matters · Safety: Reduces the risk of catastrophic fires that can endanger workers and damage facilities. · Regulatory Compliance: Many industries require fire-resistant fluids to meet safety codes. · Operational Continuity: Minimizes downtime caused by fire-related incidents. Fire Resistant vs. Flame Retardant vs. Fire Proof: What’s the Difference? · Fire Resistant: Fluids that resist ignition and burn slowly under extreme conditions. · Flame Retardant: Additives in the fluid reduce flame spread but may not prevent ignition. · Fire Proof: Implies a material cannot burn at all—this is not achievable with hydraulic fluids. Fire-resistant fluids offer the best practical protection by combining safety and performance. QUINTOLUBRIC® 888-46: A Fire-Resistant Hydraulic Fluid Solution QUINTOLUBRIC® 888-46 is a synthetic, fire-resistant hydraulic fluid designed specifically for demanding industrial hydraulic applications. It performs key functions such as: · Acting as an energy transfer medium for hydraulic machines. · Providing excellent lubrication and sealing for metal components. · Serving as a coolant to protect metal equipment from overheating. · Efficiently carrying contaminants away to maintain system cleanliness. Typical equipment benefiting from QUINTOLUBRIC® 888-46 includes: · Forklifts · Hydraulic cranes · Scissor lifts · Pallet jacks · And other hydraulic-powered machinery in harsh environments Its fire-resistant nature and synthetic base help protect your investment and ensure safer operation in high-risk settings. Choosing the Right Hydraulic Fluid for Your Operation When selecting a hydraulic fluid, consider: · Viscosity requirements based on your machine’s operating temperature and pressure. · Synthetic vs. mineral base oils depending on your need for thermal stability and longevity. · Fire resistance level required by your workplace safety regulations. · Equipment type and typical operating conditions. A high-quality fire-resistant synthetic fluid like QUINTOLUBRIC® 888-46 can meet these needs and provide peace of mind. Final Thoughts: Protect Your Equipment and People with the Right Hydraulic Fluid Hydraulic fluids do far more than just keep machinery moving—they protect, cool, and safeguard vital equipment while reducing safety risks. Understanding viscosity, synthetic base oils, and fire resistance helps you make informed decisions that improve productivity and protect your workforce. title: What is a VoIP phone (and how does it work)?
summary: A VoIP phone makes calls over the internet instead of a phone line. Learn how VoIP works, what a VoIP number is, and what drives call quality.
body_text: What is a VoIP phone (and how does it work)? A VoIP phone is any device that makes and receives calls over an internet connection instead of a traditional phone line. That device can be a desk phone that looks like a landline, an app on your laptop, your mobile phone, or a browser tab. What makes it a VoIP phone is where the audio travels: as data packets across the internet, rather than as an electrical signal down a copper pair. That's the basics, but it gets interesting when you look at the parts that decide whether your calls sound good, reach 911 correctly, and survive a security audit. That's what this covers. Key takeaways A VoIP phone sends voice as data packets over an IP network instead of using the circuit-switched public telephone network (PSTN). VoIP uses two protocols, one for setup and one for audio. SIP negotiates the call, and RTP carries the sound. Call quality depends on three numbers: Latency under 150 ms one-way, jitter under 30 ms, and packet loss under 1%. What is a VoIP phone? A VoIP phone is a device or application that transmits voice as digital data over an internet connection, using Voice over Internet Protocol. The call never touches the copper network unless it needs to reach someone who's still on it. Two VoIP endpoints talking to each other stay entirely on IP. When a VoIP caller dials a landline or a mobile number, a gateway hands the call off to the PSTN. VoIP stands for Voice over Internet Protocol. You'll also see it written as IP telephony, internet telephony, or voice over IP. They all describe the same thing: Carrying voice traffic over packet-switched IP networks rather than the circuit-switched PSTN. Types of VoIP phones VoIP phones can take several forms: Hard phones: Desk phones that look like traditional handsets but plug into ethernet or Wi-Fi instead of a phone jack. Common in call centers and offices. Softphones: Applications running on a laptop or desktop. Microsoft Teams, Zoom, and browser-based dialers all fall here. Mobile VoIP: Apps on a smartphone that place calls over cellular data or Wi-Fi rather than the carrier's voice network. WhatsApp and FaceTime work this way. ATA adapters: A small box that converts an analog phone into a VoIP endpoint, so existing handsets keep working. Conference and room devices: Speakerphones and video bars that register to a VoIP system the same way a desk phone does. VoIP phones vs. traditional phones VoIP phones and traditional phones have quite a few differences for fulfilling a relatively similar purpose. Here are the main differences: Pricing: Cloud-based VoIP calls are cheaper than traditional phone landline calls. Plus, most customers and businesses already have internet installed, so while VoIP demands additional usage fees, you won’t be purchasing additional services. Features: VoIP providers offer several advanced features you won’t find with traditional phones, like automated attendants, call parking, call flipping, real-time analytics, business integrations, and more. Device flexibility: Traditional phones are often limited to a specific physical location, while VoIP phones can be your desktop, desk phone, or on-the-go mobile device. Emergency services: VoIP phone numbers are location-dependent, so dispatchers don’t always know where to send emergency services unless the caller provides the details during a call. This makes traditional phones a more reliable system for emergency calls. Call quality and reliability: VoIP calls rely on a strong internet connection, which used to be less accessible years ago. However, you can now find reliable bandwidth in most locations, making VoIP phones just as reliable and high quality as traditional phones. Scalability: Scaling VoIP phone systems is simple—you can purchase additional lines and licenses and enable your employees’ personal devices. However, scaling traditional phones is a bit more complex—you’ll need to purchase more phone sets and wired phone lines to add more users to your system. How do VoIP phones work? At a high level, a VoIP phone converts your voice into data, sends it across the internet, and converts it back to audio on the other end. The detail that most explanations skip is that this happens over two separate protocols doing two separate jobs. Signaling and media are different things SIP (Session Initiation Protocol) handles signaling. It's the part that finds the other party, rings their phone, negotiates what audio format both sides can speak, and tears the call down when someone hangs up. SIP carries no audio at all. RTP (Real-time Transport Protocol) carries the media. Once SIP has negotiated the session, the actual voice packets flow over RTP, usually directly between the two endpoints. This split matters in practice. When a call connects but nobody can hear anything, the problem is almost always RTP being blocked by a firewall or mangled by NAT while SIP passes through fine. Knowing which protocol failed tells you where to look. Here's the full sequence: Registration: Your phone tells the VoIP provider where it is, and authenticates. Invitation: You dial. Your phone sends a SIP INVITE toward the destination. Negotiation: Both sides exchange the codecs and network addresses they can use. Media flow: The call connects. Audio is sampled, encoded, packetized, and sent over RTP, typically in 20 ms chunks. Decoding: The receiving device buffers the packets, reorders anything that arrived out of sequence, and plays the audio. Teardown: Someone hangs up, a SIP BYE goes out, and the session ends. Codecs and what they cost you The codec decides the tradeoff between bandwidth and sound quality. G.711: Uncompressed, around 64 kbps of payload before overhead. Best quality of the legacy codecs, and the default on most PSTN interconnects. G.722: Wideband, or HD voice. Same bandwidth as G.711, noticeably richer audio, though both endpoints have to support it. Opus: Adaptive and modern. Adjusts its bitrate to network conditions in real time. The standard for WebRTC and browser-based calling. G.729: Heavily compressed at around 8 kbps of payload. Useful on constrained links, at the cost of audible quality loss. Real-world bandwidth runs higher than the payload number because of IP, UDP, and RTP headers. Budget roughly 85 to 100 kbps per concurrent G.711 call in each direction. What determines VoIP call quality VoIP call quality comes down to three network measurements. Get them inside these ranges and calls sound clean. Miss them and no amount of provider-switching helps. Latency: The one-way delay between speaking and being heard. The ITU-T G.114 recommendation puts the ceiling for good quality at 150 ms one-way. Between 150 and 300 ms, people start talking over each other. Past 300 ms, the conversation stops feeling like a conversation. Jitter: The variation in packet arrival times. Under 30 ms is the working target. Jitter buffers smooth out small variations by holding packets briefly before playback, which trades a little latency for stability. Packet loss: Voice tolerates less than 1% loss before it becomes audible as clipping or dropouts. Unlike a file transfer, there's no time to retransmit a lost voice packet, so it's gone. MOS (Mean Opinion Score): A 1 to 5 quality rating. Above 4.0 is considered good. G.711 under clean conditions tops out around 4.4, which is the practical ceiling for standard voice. Bandwidth is rarely the constraint. A single call needs under 100 kbps, which any broadband connection handles. The problems come from a network that's fast on average and inconsistent under load, which is why QoS rules that prioritize voice traffic tend to fix more calls than a bigger pipe does. If you're running voice at scale, instrument it. Twilio Voice Insights surfaces these metrics per call, so you can tell the difference between a bad provider and a bad Wi-Fi access point. Should you use a VoIP phone system? VoIP phone systems offer significant advantages over traditional phone landline systems, but these aren't right for everyone. Here are a few benefits and drawbacks you should consider before investing in your business communications system: Benefits of VoIP phones Call routing: Easily route your calls to a VoIP phone, regardless of where you've plugged in your physical network. This allows you to take calls anywhere in the world, as long as you have a reliable internet connection. Portable numbers: Since VoIP numbers are virtual, you can take them wherever you go. That means you keep the same number anywhere in the world. Lower costs: Because VoIP doesn't require investments in traditional private branch exchange or PBX systems and landlines, you can switch and save significantly on your phone bill. Plain old telephone services (POTS) cost your business each month for each line, while VoIP saves you money with pay-as-you-go pricing . This allows you to easily scale up or down in response to demand. Clearer quality: Thanks to the evolution of the internet, finding a high-quality connection is simple and easy. This leads to clear calls with no noticeable latency, lag, or dropouts. However, if you don't have a quality connection, VoIP can become a con (more on that later). Multichannel functionality: SIP trunking enables you to provision SMS and MMS functionality from your phone numbers, allowing you to send texts, images, and videos—creating a more seamless conversation. Security and privacy: VoIP technology can eliminate security and privacy threats with encryptions and identity management advancements. Plus, with Twilio Voice Insights , you can analyze your call performance to troubleshoot customer issues faster and deliver better communication experiences. While VoIP has a number of benefits, it's not all sunshine and rainbows. There are a few downsides to VoIP that you should keep in mind. Drawbacks of VoIP phones Quality dependent on internet connection: VoIP is only as reliable as your internet connection. While VoIP doesn't require too much bandwidth, you'll still need low latency on your network for lag-free conversations. Limitations for emergency services: The 911 system is built with traditional phones in mind. So when you dial 911, first responders will be alerted to the fixed location of your landline. However, with the portability of VoIP calling, calling 911 will only transmit the address you provided at the time of setup—not your current location. Of course, you could provide your location details when making the 911 call, but that's not always a possibility in an emergency. Power dependency: If you lose power and have no backup solution, your VoIP phones won't work. However, landlines don't require local electricity to make calls—they rely on power sent through the landline from the power companies. These companies usually have backup generators in case of a broad power outage, allowing you to keep making calls. What to look for in a VoIP provider Not every VoIP provider offers the right set of features and functionality for your business. Some VoIP providers simply offer additional phone numbers and call-forwarding features, while others enable SMS, team messaging, file sharing, and call management features. Here are a few things you’ll want to consider when looking for the right VoIP provider: Price: Think about whether you can afford the VoIP provider's different tiers. Some charge for more advanced features, while others provide free international calling to select destinations. Examine your budget and determine what you can afford now and at scale. Scalability: Consider how big you plan to grow your team and customer base. Some systems cater to small teams, while others support big businesses with hundreds or thousands of employees. Features: Think about what features you’ll need to support your team and provide top-notch experiences for your customers. This could be IVR systems , multilevel automated attendants, call parking, video conferencing, and (possibly, most important) APIs, SDKs , and integrations. Channel support: Consider what channels you plan on using for your business. If you’re just looking for voice systems, you can go for cheaper options. However, if you want to add SMS, video conferencing, team messaging, WhatsApp, Facebook Messenger, and live streaming, you’ll need a more advanced VoIP provider. Build a VoIP system with Twilio Consumers and businesses alike are dropping old landline technology in favor of wireless and VoIP-enabled phones, and it's not hard to see why. Businesses that adopt this technology now will have success for years to come and get access to all the VoIP advantages we shared. With flexible voice pricing options , there's no reason to delay making the switch. Want to get started? Check out all our no-code voice apps that you can build in less than 5 minutes. Plus, take a look at how you can build a VoIP system with Twilio, 3CX, and Python . Frequently asked questions Q: What does VoIP stand for and what does it mean? A: VoIP stands for Voice Over Internet Protocol. It's a technology that lets you make and receive phone calls using the internet instead of traditional phone lines. Think of it as turning your voice into data that travels over the web. Q: Do VoIP phones work during power outages? A: No, VoIP phones need electricity and internet to function. Unlike traditional landlines that get power through the phone line itself, VoIP systems stop working when you lose power unless you have a backup power source like a UPS battery. Q: Can I keep my existing phone number with VoIP? A: Yes, most VoIP providers allow you to port (transfer) your existing phone number to their service. This process typically takes 1-3 business days and lets you keep the same number customers already know. Q: How much internet speed do I need for VoIP calls? A: VoIP requires minimal bandwidth—about 64-100 kbps per call for good quality. A typical broadband connection easily handles multiple simultaneous VoIP calls without affecting other internet activities. Q: Are VoIP calls as clear as regular phone calls? A: With a good internet connection, VoIP calls often sound clearer than traditional phones. However, call quality depends entirely on your internet speed and stability—poor connections result in choppy, delayed audio. Q: Can I use my existing desk phones with VoIP? A: Sometimes. You can use traditional phones with an adapter (ATA device) or upgrade to IP phones designed specifically for VoIP systems. Many businesses prefer IP phones for better features and integration. Q. Are VoIP calls secure? VoIP calls are secure when encryption is enabled. SIP over TLS protects the signaling, and SRTP encrypts the audio itself. Without both, call metadata and audio are readable on the network. Toll fraud is the other common risk, mitigated with rate limits and anomaly alerting.

title: What is Cloud-based CRM? Benefits, Costs, and Top Solutions

Benefits, Costs, and Top Solutions Last updated: July 2026 Cloud-based CRM solutions have gained traction as businesses seek more flexible and scalable customer management systems in 2026. These platforms support remote work trends and aim to reduce IT overhead. What is a cloud-based CRM? A cloud-based CRM is a customer relationship management software hosted on a provider's servers, accessible via the internet. This model eliminates the need for on-premise infrastructure, offering scalable solutions that suit various business sizes and needs. How does cloud-based CRM work? Cloud-based CRM systems operate by hosting data and applications on the provider's servers, allowing users to access these services via web browsers or dedicated apps. This model removes the need for businesses to maintain on-site hardware and infrastructure, facilitating a smooth and scalable CRM experience. Typically, these systems employ a subscription-based pricing model, enabling companies to pay based on their needs rather than making substantial upfront investments. Cloud hosting through provider servers is a core aspect of how cloud-based CRMs function. This setup means that the CRM’s infrastructure, including databases and backend systems, is managed off-site by the service provider in secure data centers. As a result, businesses can avoid the complexities of maintaining physical servers and focus on using the CRM’s features for their customer relationship management tasks. Accessibility is a prominent benefit offered by cloud-based CRMs. By enabling access through web browsers and dedicated apps, these systems allow team members to interact with the CRM data from various devices, such as desktops, laptops, tablets, and smartphones. This accessibility ensures that sales teams, customer service representatives, and managers can update information, track customer interactions, and generate reports from anywhere with an internet connection. Such flexibility enhances collaboration and ensures that critical data is always at hand. The subscription-based model inherent in cloud CRMs offers a financial advantage by spreading costs over time instead of requiring a hefty initial investment. Businesses typically select from a range of pricing tiers, which may vary based on user capabilities, storage limits, and support options. This model is particularly advantageous for small to medium enterprises (SMEs) that prefer predictable monthly or annual expenses over capital expenditures. FALLING WATERS, W.Va., July 08, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- LGI Homes proudly announces the grand opening of The Meadows at Riverside, an exciting new single-family home community located in Falling Waters. This highly anticipated neighborhood offers thoughtfully designed homes featuring modern upgrades, spacious layouts and exceptional value in a scenic riverside setting. The Meadows at Riverside delivers a lifestyle centered on comfort, convenience and outdoor recreation. Nestled among the natural beauty of Falling Waters, residents will enjoy a welcoming community featuring walking paths, pickleball courts, a children’s playground, gazebo, barbecue grills and open green spaces. Outdoor enthusiasts will appreciate the close proximity to Falling Waters Waterfalls Park, the Potomac River and other local parks offering hiking, kayaking, picnicking and year-round recreation. Centrally located between Martinsburg and Hagerstown, The Meadows at Riverside is a short drive to everyday conveniences. Residents can enjoy a day of shopping at Valley Mall or Crosspoint Shopping Center less than 10 miles from the community. Major commuter routes including I-70, I-81 and US-11, as well as the MARC train station, are also nearby. "The Meadows at Riverside offers homebuyers an incredible opportunity to enjoy modern living in one of West Virginia's most desirable locations," stated Vice President of Operations Paul DiConsiglio. "With thoughtfully designed homes, included upgrades, outstanding community amenities and a simplified path to homeownership, this community is designed to help families achieve their dream of owning a home." The community features a collection of spacious three- and four-bedroom single-family homes, each complete with attached two-car garages and flexible floor plans designed to fit a variety of lifestyles. Every home includes LGI Homes' CompleteHome Plus™ package, offering a full suite of upgrades at no additional cost. These enhancements include granite countertops, a tile backsplash, stainless steel Whirlpool® kitchen appliances, designer cabinetry, luxury vinyl plank flooring, Wi-Fi-enabled garage door openers, programmable Honeywell thermostats, energy-efficient features and professionally designed exterior details. Six thoughtfully designed floor plans are available at The Meadows at Riverside: Martin – 3 beds, 2 baths, 2-car garage, 1,527 sq. ft. Allen – 3 beds, 2 baths, 2-car garage, 1,656 sq. ft. Birch – 3 beds, 2.5 baths, 2-car garage, 1,742 sq. ft. Craven – 4 beds, 2.5 baths, 2-car garage, 2,397 sq. ft. Davidson – 4 beds, 2.5 baths, 2-car garage, 1,800 sq. ft. Rolen – 4 beds, 2.5 baths, 2-car garage, 2,294 sq. ft. With its upgraded interiors, outstanding amenities, convenient location and welcoming atmosphere, The Meadows at Riverside is poised to become one of the premier new home communities in the Falling Waters area. A grand opening event will be held on the weekend of July 11 & 12, 2026 with limited-time savings available at the event. Interested buyers are encouraged to contact the LGI Homes Information Center at (833) 788-0974 ext 56 for additional details. LGI Homes has closed over 80,000 homes since its founding in 2003 and has delivered profitable financial results every year. Nationally recognized for its quality construction and exceptional customer service, LGI Homes was named to Newsweek’s list of the World’s Most Trustworthy Companies.
